title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
ai_summary: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making . But recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem . We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly .

title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.
ai_summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning . They have been used as high-level planners for embodied AI . But physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states .

title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($ρ^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.
ai_summary: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect . In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under cross-validation .

title: RepProbe: Can Video Language Models Count Repeated Actions? A Diagnostic Benchmark
abstract: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/
ai_summary: State-of-the-art video language models fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats . RepProbe is a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions .

title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
ai_summary: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop . ChunkAct introduces action chunking to agentic robotics . Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously .

title: AegisAsync: Symbolic Async-Event Simulation for Risks in Python Asynchronous Programs
abstract: Security and robustness risks in Python async programs depend on event order, object identity, and execution after exceptions or cancellation. Detecting these risks requires connecting related operations across function calls and tracking their effects along execution paths. We present AegisAsync, a bytecode-based analysis of Python async risks for CPython 3.10-3.14. Its Async Event Transition Graph combines bytecode control flow, resolved calls, async events, and symbolic object relations. Bounded path-local simulation tracks event order and object states and explores cancellation at await suspensions. Six detector plugins evaluate the resulting traces and states to produce candidates with supporting witnesses. On AsyncBench, our benchmark of 180 labeled risks, AegisAsync detects all labeled risks with zero false positives on each of the five versions. Across five path budgets on 2,500 PyPI package versions, source review confirms 457 of 910 AegisAsync candidate records (50.2%), representing 457 unique bugs; across three flake8-async samples, 70 of 2,187 review judgments are confirmed (3.2%). By submission, 166 PoCs reproduce AegisAsync findings, and we have reported 157 bugs to developers, of which 16 have been confirmed and fixed.
ai_summary: Security and robustness risks in Python async programs depend on event order, object identity, and execution after exceptions or cancellation . Detecting these risks requires connecting related operations across function calls and tracking their effects along execution paths .

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.
ai_summary: The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD . We recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers .

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. Our 3D foundation model, anatomix, is used to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes, and we further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system won first place in the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at http://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.
ai_summary: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems . They can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings .

title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
ai_summary: AesCode generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance . To do so, Aes code represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable .

title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
abstract: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/

title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
ai_summary: DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy . The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted by a verbose thinker .

title: Visual Tokens on Demand: Visual Budgeting for Scalable and Efficient Multi-Image Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.

Existing techniques that address the above issue include visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, and visualToken compression. Existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient

title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. title: The Last Remote Sensing Model Built by Humans? Casting Any Earth Observation Task as Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Earth observation (EO) models are still built by hand. For each new task, experts design a training recipe and tune it against a benchmark. We show that this loop can be handed to an agent. Any verifiable task can be cast as a harness and a verifier, where the harness defines what the agent may use and the verifier defines what counts as success. Every EO task can be made verifiable, through labeled benchmarks, independent sensors, physical models or the repeated observation of the same place. Given only these two components, a general-purpose coding agent builds the EO model and improves it recursively on its own outputs. Settings long treated as separate research problems, from learning with a handful of labels to adapting across domains, become choices of harness and verifier. On four EO benchmarks spanning optical, SAR and multispectral time-series imagery, agent-built models surpass the state of the art and keep most of that accuracy from about 1% of the training labels. This establishes a new paradigm for EO, in which people design harnesses and verifiers and agents build the models, so EO models improve as agents do.

abstract: Accurate carbohydrate estimation is critical for insulin dosing in individuals with diabetes on multiple daily injections. Conventional methods such as visual estimation and food exchange systems are inconsistent, particularly in multicultural Asian settings where portion sizes vary and nutritional labeling is limited. NutriDish is an AI-powered system designed to automates carbohydrate estimation from food images. This study compared the accuracy of carbohydrate estimates generated by NutriDish and ChatGPT-5 against reference values established by a dietitian using weighed food portions. Between July and August 2025, food items were collected from hawker centers, food courts, restaurants, and homes, supermarkets, and convenience stores across Singapore to capture the region's diverse culinary landscape. Items were classified as simple foods or composite meals. NutriDish and ChatGPT-5 independently estimated carbohydrate content, while a dietitian established reference values using weighing portions and a validated nutrient database. Accuracy was assessed using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), proportion of estimates within ± 10 g of the reference value, and Bland-Altman analysis. Across 150 food items, NutriDish achieved significantly lower MAE [5.9 ± 5.3 g (median: 4.1 g, IQR: 1.0-9.0) vs. 8.7 ± 7.4 g (median: 6.0 g, IQR: 3.0-13.4);  NutriDish demonstrated good agreement with dietitian-derived carbohydrate estimates, highlighting its potential to aid carbohydrate counting in individuals treated with insulin. Future studies should evaluate real-world clinical usability, integration into diabetes self-management ecosystems and impact on long-term glycemic control.

title: AI-driven multi-omics biomarkers in precision breast cancer therapeutics: from discovery to clinical translation.
abstract: Breast cancer is biologically heterogeneous, yet conventional clinical decisions rely on static, single-marker proxies (ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67) that capture only a narrow slice of tumor biology. This mini-review argues that AI-driven multi-omics biomarkers offer a valuable shift toward systems-level, model-derived probabilities integrating genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and imaging information to explain and predict disease behavior more faithfully. We synthesize recent advances across three domains: (i) computational strategies for multi-omics integration, from classical penalized regression and ensemble learning to deep multimodal architectures and foundation-model embeddings; (ii) therapeutically relevant biomarker classes across tissue, liquid biopsy, and imaging modalities; and (iii) emerging pathways for embedding these biomarkers into clinical decision support. We highlight validation, interpretability, and robust handling of missing modalities as prerequisites for clinical trust, and outline how biomarker-driven trials, standardized reporting (e.g., TRIPOD + AI), and privacy-preserving data consortia can move AI-driven multi-omics biomarkers toward clinical and regulatory maturity.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Diagnostic and Triage Accuracy in Hospital Emergency Departments: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Emergency departments face challenges of overcrowding and human error. This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving triage and diagnostic accuracy in emergency settings. This systematic review was conducted by searching PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar until September 2025. Inclusion criteria comprised original studies reporting at least one quantitative performance metric. Study quality was assessed using NOS and QUADAS-2. Data were synthesized narratively. AI models outperformed traditional triage systems (AUC often >0.90). In clinical interpretation of AUC, its limitations in imbalanced datasets should be considered, and metrics such as PPV, NPV, and AUPRC should also be reported. For instance, despite an acceptable AUC, ChatGPT 4.0 led to significant over-triage due to low specificity (18.2%). However, risks of algorithmic bias and challenges of integrating AI with real-world clinical workflows remain major implementation barriers. User resistance and the need for continuous ethical oversight were also identified. AI holds potential to improve emergency triage, but current evidence is largely based on retrospective single-center studies. Clinical implementation should be gradual, starting in high-risk domains (e.g., sepsis screening), and supported by continuous ethical oversight.

title: A Scoping Review of Challenges and Solutions in the Successful Implementation of Hospital Management Information Systems (HMIS).
abstract: A Hospital Management Information System (HMIS) is a comprehensive, computer-based system designed to manage and streamline the entire spectrum of hospital operations, including administrative, clinical, and financial processes. After duplicate removal, 361 titles and abstracts were screened according to the eligibility criteria. Following full-text assessment, 18 studies were relevant to the research objective. Four categories of key factors in successful HMIS implementation were identified, including technical, organizational, human, and environmental factors. The proposed solutions include advanced security measures, phased implementation, comprehensive user training, and strong leadership support. The results showed that a multidimensional approach that can simultaneously address technical, organizational, human, and environmental factors is crucial for successful HMIS implementation. Employing targeted strategies to overcome these challenges and improve the efficiency of hospital information management is essential, as these strategies were identified. It should also focus on localizing strategies related to these factors in line with the country-specific challenges and solutions in different healthcare settings.

title: Hybrid multi-model framework with knowledge distillation for precise and efficient sickle cell detection.
abstract: Accurate and timely detection of sickle red blood cells has a significant impact on the patients' treatment. Developing a computer vision system that is both lightweight and resource-efficient is important for enabling real-time edge-based applications in resource-constrained healthcare environments. This study proposes a hybrid sickle cell detection framework that uses Bi-lightweight Knowledge Distillation (KD)-guided CNNs, combining two lightweight student models from different teacher networks with Machine Learning (ML) classifiers to identify sickle cells with accuracy and efficiency. Using depthwise separable convolution layers, lightweight models are created that drastically lower model complexity. These lightweight models are improved by extracting knowledge from top-performing teacher networks, such as MobileNetV2 and DenseNet121. Using this Knowledge Distillation learning technique, lightweight models can enhance their representational capabilities without adding to their computational complexity. To improve decision-making performance, the Bi-distilled student models are combined with conventional machine learning KNN classifiers to create a hybrid ensemble that combines the advantages of ML-based classification with dual KD-guided CNN-based feature extraction. The Sickle Cell Disease Dataset is used to train and validate the proposed system. The learned student models are then converted into TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) format using Float32 quantization to further reduce computational complexity. In combination with dual KD-guided CNN models and a KNN classifier, the proposed hybrid model achieves a high classification accuracy of 95.45% and an F1-score of 95.02% while being small at only 3.96 MB. Deploying and evaluating the framework on a resource-constrained Raspberry Pi 4 Model B demonstrate its potential for real-time, edge-based, and point-of-care applications.
